philosophy_summary: 狗不叫 (财主) is a Hong Kong value-and-income investor whose edge is the disciplined fusion of fundamental conviction with a covered/cash-secured option-selling overlay, executed inside an intimate command of HKEX mechanics and the HK/China tax code. His core stance is owner-not-trader: he buys cash-generative, high-dividend HK blue chips (oil majors, telecoms, insurers, select internet names), holds through drawdowns judged on a total-return (dividends-included) basis, and judges the 'bull market' by per-share equity and dividend growth rather than price. Around that core he runs a non-directional premium program — selling puts only at strikes where he genuinely wants the shares (and has the full cash to take delivery) and selling modest covered calls for 'pocket-money' volatility income. The whole apparatus is governed by one hard bottom line: no leverage, ever. He sizes puts to deliverable cash (often to incoming dividends, keeping the program self-financing), bounds every single-name worst case to a small fraction of the book, refuses fat premiums on names with 'no floor', and avoids exotic structures (accumulators) whose maximum loss he cannot state. He anchors strikes to fundamental price floors, rolls down for net credit while accounting for HK stamp duty and commissions, and times expiries around ex-dividend dates. His second, rarer edge is mechanical and fiscal: he knows that HK options need a non-Connect broker, that red-chips escape dividend tax via physical-certificate conversion while H-shares cannot, that special vs ordinary dividends adjust strikes differently, and that HK option liquidity lives in only a few mega-caps. Behaviorally he prizes holding mentality at bottoms, the discipline of inaction after deep research, diversification over consensus concentration, owner-style AGM activism, and skepticism toward corporate denials, engineered rallies, and unenacted policy. He is candid about path-dependence and his own errors, marking sector theses (EVs, holdco discounts) to evidence. Honesty about attribution — option income is only ~1.9% of the book — keeps the overlay in its proper, modest place.
